title: Trump’s Move to Rescind Roadless Rule Rewards Logging and Mining Interests
author: Matt Sedlar
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/clearcuts-1-680x581.png)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/08/28/trumps-
move-to-rescind-roadless-rule-rewards-logging-and-mining-interests/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/clearcuts-1-680x581.png)

Industrial clearcutting in the Oregon Coast Range. Photo: Jeffrey St. Clair.

Last week, US Department of Agriculture (USDA) Secretary Brook L. Rollins
[moved forward](https://www.usda.gov/about-usda/news/press-
releases/2026/08/18/usda-acts-remove-roadless-rule-restrictions-exacerbate-
rising-wildfire-risk) on the agency’s promise to revoke the [2001 Roadless
Rule](https://www.fs.usda.gov/managing-land/planning/roadless/archive),
opening a [public comment
period](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/08/20/2026-16965/special-
areas-roadless-area-conservation) on the proposal and a draft environmental
statement on its impact. If this sounds familiar, that’s because we [covered
this](https://cepr.net/publications/rushed-public-comment-process-raises-red-
flags/) almost a year ago during the scoping process.

So what’s changed, and what hasn’t?

First, it’s important to understand what the Roadless Rule does. Enacted at
the end of the Clinton administration, the rule prohibits road construction,
road reconstruction, and timber harvesting on 58.5 million acres of roadless
areas within the National Forests. The [environmental impact
statement](https://www.fs.usda.gov/sites/default/files/roadless/roadless-feis-
ssummary.pdf) at the time argued that protecting these areas would maintain
sources of clean drinking water for nearby communities, support habitats for
native plant and animal species, and conserve biological diversity.

Since its passage, the rule has faced legal
[pushback](https://www.fs.usda.gov/managing-
land/planning/roadless/archive#:~:text=September,36%20KB) from states and
corporations, including mining and logging interests. And since 2001, some
states have established their own regulations. More than 9 million acres in
[Idaho](https://www.fs.usda.gov/r04/planning/roadless-area-idaho-rule) and
over 4 million acres in [Colorado](https://www.fs.usda.gov/r02/natural-
resources/forest-management/colorado-roadless-rule) are exempt from the rule
because the states have passed specific legislation that supersedes the
federal regulations. The state rules, however, protect some areas while
opening up others to [expanding
recreation](https://www.postindependent.com/news/colorado-wilderness-usda-
roadless-rule-repeal/), like skiing, and [logging and mining
activities](https://www.wilderness.org/articles/article/conserving-roadless-
areas).

In June 2025, the USDA [announced](https://cepr.net/publications/rushed-
public-comment-process-raises-red-flags/) it would begin the process of
revoking the rule. The administration claims roadless areas contribute to
deadly wildfires. According to a [statement](https://www.usda.gov/about-
usda/news/press-releases/2026/08/18/usda-acts-remove-roadless-rule-
restrictions-exacerbate-rising-wildfire-risk#:~:text=%E2%80%9CMore,2014%2E)
from US Forest Service Chief Tom Schultz, “More than 40 percent of inventoried
roadless areas, primarily in the West, have high or very high wildfire hazard
potential. And only 5 percent of those areas have received hazardous fuels
reduction treatments since 2014.” According to USDA, state-specific rules
would not be affected by USDA’s decision.

But in an earlier
[memo](https://www.usda.gov/sites/default/files/documents/implementation-
secretarial-memo-1078-006.pdf) from the US Forest Service, Acting Associate
Chief Christopher French said the quiet part out loud. French echoed Trump’s
[call](https://www.federalregister.gov/executive-order/14225) for the
immediate expansion of timber production in these areas. By August, the agency
had released
[rulemaking](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/08/29/2025-16581/special-
areas-roadless-area-conservation-national-forest-system-lands) on the
management of roadless areas on National Forest System lands, with public
comments due by September 19 — a mere 21 days. Despite the short comment
period, or perhaps because of it, the agency had received over 220,000
comments.

The agency released its [draft environmental impact
statement](https://usfs.maps.arcgis.com/home/item.html?id=c6122042b4ae46c9b323306912e8b40e#overview)
last week, which looked at three options: maintaining the existing Roadless
Rule, rescinding the rule, or removing restrictions in roaded areas and the
wildland-urban interface (WUI) while continuing to manage inventoried roadless
areas outside those areas. That last option would remove prohibitions on 31
million acres, including 17.9 million acres that are within half a mile of
existing roads or communities in the WUI, while continuing management of 13
million acres protected under the Roadless Rule. You can already guess which
option the federal government is endorsing. Again, the public has less than a
month [to submit
comments](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/08/20/2026-16965/special-
areas-roadless-area-conservation), which are due on September 21.

If that seems like a short amount of time to collect comments, it is. The time
required to collect comments can vary, of course. According to the federal
[eRulemaking Program Management Office](https://www.regulations.gov/learn),
“In a typical case, an agency will allow 60 days for public comment.” The
Federal Register
[states](https://uploads.federalregister.gov/uploads/2013/09/The-Rulemaking-
Process.pdf) that complex rulemaking processes — such as a decision that
affects millions of acres across the US — may take more than 180 days. Shorter
comment periods may be implemented if adequate justification exists. The
administration hasn’t provided a justification.

The quick turnaround — less than a year — from the scoping process to the
draft impact statement was also unusual. In theory, an environmental impact
statement should take at least two years, as stipulated by the National
Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) of 1969. The Council on Environmental Quality[
found](https://ceq.doe.gov/docs/nepa-
practice/CEQ_EIS_Timeline_Report_2025-1-13.pdf) in 2024 that the median time
from notice of intent to final impact statement was 2.2 years. And as we noted
last August, this is an incredibly complex issue that affects tens of millions
of acres of forestland and watersheds across the US.

And then there are the issues with the Forest Service’s claims about
wildfires. Schultz’s comment that only 5 percent of inventoried roadless areas
have received fuels reduction treatment has less to do with access and more to
do with funding. The US Forest Service has been [chronically
underfunded](https://morethanjustparks.substack.com/p/the-us-forest-service-
is-starving) for decades, and Trump’s attempts to dismantle it through
[staffing and further budget
cuts](https://www.wta.org/news/signpost/reorganization-budget-cuts-trail-
maintenance-could-break-usfs) have not helped. Also, researchers have found
that from 1992 to 2012, 84 percent of all wildfires were [caused by
people](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1617394114) and that building
roads in roadless areas is likely to [increase the risk of
fires](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s42408-026-00450-2).

Last week, the [Firefighters United for Safety, Ethics, and
Ecology](https://fusee.org/) released statements from experts who argue that
[smokejumpers, heli-rappelers, and helitack
crews](https://www.fs.usda.gov/sites/default/files/fs_media/fs_document/aviation-
history.pdf) can manage fires in roadless areas and that the absence of
communities or infrastructure in roadless wildlands actually provides more
opportunities to safely manage fire, especially when it can be beneficial to
the forest.

Rather than listening to experts on the matter, the administration appears
focused on its corporate donors who will profit from this decision. Hopefully,
at some point, states can [implement their own roadless area
regulations](https://cepr.net/publications/public-lands-for-private-profit/),
making it harder for future administrations to give away the land to
companies. In the meantime, we’ll probably see this battle play out in the
courts. States [can
sue](https://scholarship.law.cornell.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?referer=&httpsredir=1&article=4697&context=clr#:~:text=Accordingly%2C%20a%20State%20may%20challenge%20federal%20statutes,undermine%20the%20continued%20enforceability%20of%2C%20state%20law.&text=However%2C%20as%20both%20Part%20I%20and%20Part,may%20seek%20redress%20only%20for%20that%20harm.)
if federal mandates harm residents or infringe upon distinct state
authorities. Under USDA’s proposal, industrial expansion could threaten clean
air, water, and soil, while inadequate oversight of commercial forestry
projects could increase wildfire risk. And with the rescission of the Roadless
Rule, that’s a likely scenario.
